title: About Nothing
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of embracing emptiness, or "suchness," which means letting go of attachments to concepts like God, self, and external realities. This understanding allows us to connect with the present moment and find meaning in our lives without seeking something more. By embracing imperfection and finding comfort in our current circumstances, we can discover a sense of peace and home that is already within us, regardless of where we are or what we have.

Is that right?
So you're leaving sometime this afternoon.
Thanks for coming and sitting.
We're going to miss you.
It'll feel empty in here without you.
It feels empty in here anyway, but it'll feel even more empty without you.
So we do appreciate your coming.
Take your time going home and getting back into whatever it is you have to do.
Is anybody coming?
Some people are coming too.
Okay, that's pretty good.
Well, today I would like to talk about my favorite subject: nothing.
This is my favorite subject.
Next month, I'm going to go down to Tassajara and do a five-day retreat with Danny Matt, who's one of the great contemporary scholars of Jewish mysticism.
So we're going to do a retreat for five days together.
And he said, you make up the title.
And I said, okay.
So the title is About Nothing.
That's the title of our retreat.
Probably nobody will come.
And of course, you all know where that title comes from.
You will remember that this is the famous line of Jerry Seinfeld, who when he was asked to describe to the producers who were proposing to put his show on the air, "Well, what's your show about?"
And he said, he's a little bit, well, "it's about nothing."
And George Costanza, who was sitting there at the time in the way that he is, over the top, you know, George way, said, "Yeah, yeah, it's about nothing.
It's going to be great.
It's going to be a fabulous show."
And this was a scene in the Seinfeld show about how they started the show.
So that's where I got my title, About Nothing.
Now, nothing, I admit, doesn't sound like much.
But I do feel that nothing is very important.
When there's too much something and anything and everything and there's not enough nothing, I think we're in trouble.
Possibly this is the problem that we're having in our world.
We've got too much of everything and not enough nothing.
Nothing will never wreck the planet and start wars.
Nothing is content to be nothing.
It doesn't need anything.
In the fifth century, the Christian mystic Pseudo-Denisus wrote that although God is the cause of everything, God is nothing.
God isn't something because God is beyond all being.
And so God can't be any sort of thing.
Therefore, God must be nothing.
In the ninth century, John Scotus Aragonius used the Latin word nihil, nothing, to describe God, who created the world ex nihilo, out of nothing.
God's own substance is the basis of the world.
So essentially, the world is nothing.
And it's the job of religious practitioners to fully appreciate nothing.
And the Jewish Kabbalists were influenced by all of these thoughts.
And they had the word ayan to stand for God, ayan, which means nothing, and yesh, which means something.
And so their project was to understand the mystery, and the practice was to discover exactly how did yesh emerge from ayan.
And how is it that yesh was infused at all points with ayan?
They had the thought that everything is always changing.
And so every moment of time and transformation came about through an encounter with ayan.
In this way, the world of something is constantly being renewed by its connection with nothing.
The abyss of nothing, which maybe seems scary, is actually crossed every moment as something, or what looks to us like something, is kissed by nothing so that it can appear in this world.
So that was the effort that the Jewish mystics were always making in their practice of prayer and meditation.
To forget, that's what they called it, forgetting, to forget or unknow so that they could fully merge their souls with nothing.

This might sound a little foreboding or weird, and I think the mystics of the Kabbalah thought that it was foreboding and weird themselves, but they also saw it as something inherently necessary and positive.
And they saw, and maybe we feel this way ourselves, that the world, relentlessly being something, something, something every minute, is too much.
The world without nothing is too oppressive.
It's too heavy and hard to bear.
But that world isn't the real world, the mystics felt.
It's a world in exile from itself, in exile from its inherent divinity.

And they thought that it was their job, through their spiritual efforts and through their lifelong endeavors, to wake up the exiled world, to bring it home, to liberate it so that the impossible would once again become possible in this physical world.
And by the 18th century or so, Jewish mysticism underwent a big change.
It became democratic and less secret (it used to be really secret and esoteric), and it became more everyday.
And it became more participatory and more joyful and more experiential and more psychological, less philosophical or linguistic speculation.
So that was the Hasidic movement, which was really a development of Jewish mysticism.
So here's a quotation from Dov Baer, the Magid of Mezrich, who was one of the great Hasidic rabbis.
He said:
*The essence of the worship of God is to attain the state of humility.

The essence of the worship of God is to attain the state of humility, namely to understand that all one's physical and mental powers and one's essential being are dependent on the divine elements within.
One is simply a channel for the divine attributes.
And one attains such humility through the awe of God's vastness, through realizing that there is no place empty of God.
And then one comes to the state of Ayin, nothing, which is the state of humility, radical humility.
One has no independent self and is contained, as it were, in creation.*
So this is what the Christian and Jewish mystics were thinking about through the lens of the deep faith that they had in their traditions.
They were looking at the world and the only thing they could see was God.
And then they were trying to look into the face of God and the only thing they could see was this world.
And they considered the process of seeing the world as God, and the world and God as the same in nothingness.
They considered that vision and that practice as the process of their lives, of really being human and living in the world and acting in the world, as though there were actually nothing but God.

There's a sign over the garden at Gethsemane Monastery in Kentucky, Thomas Merton's monastery, that says, "Nothing but God," which means nothing but nothing, which means that all of our human problems, however compelling they may seem, actually amount to nothing.
All of our problems, all of our challenges are only God working out God's destiny in us.
One of the greatest of all Christian mystics was Meister Eckhart, who was a 14th century German preacher, fiery and eloquent.
And he was in this profound tradition of reflecting on nothing.
And he said a lot of pretty outrageous things about this, so that after he died he was sort of excommunicated from the church because it was too much.
But here's one quotation from Meister Eckhart:
*Before there were any creatures, God was not God.
Now, I say that God, as far as God is God, is not the perfected end of created beings.
So therefore, we beg God to rid us of God, so we may grasp and rejoice in that everlasting truth in which the highest angel and the tiniest fly and the soul are equal.
And I pray to God that God will rid me of God, for my real being is more than God.*
This is shocking.
No wonder the church fathers didn't like this.
So I don't know what you think of all this.
I'm telling you all these quotations.
I don't know how you feel about this.
Maybe you don't like it.
Maybe the God language is a little offensive to some people.

Because in these days, we come to a moment in which so many people have experienced so much pain from the word God, while so many other people have been saved from their despair and their addiction and everything by God, that we can barely mention the word God in mixed company without creating all kinds of a stir.
But anyway, let us not forget that it's just a word after all.
It's absolutely nothing to worry about.
Yes, why would one worry about nothing?
Nothing is just nothing after all.
But perhaps you might have felt, as I did, some similarity in our practice to all this.
To me, it seems actually quite similar.
We understand our life as being just our life.
Nothing special.
But at the same time, we know that our life is beyond our life.
And we understand death as being unforgettable and terrible news.
And at the same time, also, good news.
And we also understand, I believe, and from time to time, feel quite touched by the sacredness of each and every thing.
In Zen, we call this suchness.
Tata.
T-A-T-H-A.
Just this.
It's the same this that the monastics were asking about in yesterday's story.
"Is this also destroyed?"
And this, this is not something out there.
Thinking there's something more real out there somewhere is a big problem.
It causes a lot of suffering.
And that's why Meister Eckhart prays that God will rid him of God, will rid him of this concept that there's something outside of him more than him.
It's noteworthy that he doesn't get rid of God himself.
He prays that God will please get rid of God.
Anyway, that's what he means.

Just this moment.

And that's God.
Coming, going.
Right here.
Wherever you are.
Forever.
Just like this.
In this moment of your life, it absolutely could not be any other way.

Subjunctive maybe.
We have things that we could say like, it could be.
It could have been.
It should have been.
It might have been.
And we have this wonderful word, two little letters: if.
Sometimes we use it as another word: if only.
If only.

But they also send us scurrying in painful pursuit of dreams.
Actually, there is no other place than here.
And there is no other time than now.
Every place we could ever visit is here.
Every time in which we could ever experience life is now.
Even if, here and now, we are wondering about what might have been.
Even then, we are Tathagata.
More than God, as Eckhart says.
Of course, as we all well understand, Buddhism is not a theistic religion.
When Buddhism was first introduced to Western cultures, people were confused.
And I think even to some extent today, confused about is Buddhism a religion or not.
Because as we understand, a religion is a belief in a supreme being of some sort.
And the different religions have different ideas and so on about which supreme being and how the supreme being is and so on.
So could it be a religion if there is no supreme being?
Buddha somehow never got into the idea of whether there was a supreme being and what kind of a supreme being it was.
I mean, in the early suttas, there are all kinds of gods appearing to the Buddha right and left.
But somehow it doesn't seem all that important.
It's not what the Buddha was concerned about.
The Buddha was concerned about suffering.
He was concerned about the suffering of regular people like you and me.
He was not concerned with ultimate and important questions.
He considered them, in the light of the problem of human suffering, profoundly distracting.
And as we know, famously when he was asked these sorts of questions, he would simply remain silent.
This is not to say that Buddha had no views or ideas.
He did.
He had counter views.
That is, he identified important views that human beings typically held.
Views that kept us chained to our suffering.
Views that we held without even knowing that we hold them.
And he proposed counter views.
Views that would undo the pain of the views we already held.
Of course, when you propose counter views, this can backfire on you.
And you can contrive to bind yourself up in the counter views just as nicely as you bound yourself up in your previous views.
Something that the Buddha tried mightily to avoid, and the Zen Masters tried even more mightily to avoid this problem.
But in the end, sometimes nothing works.
Because as we all know, human pain is incredibly persuasive.
Incredibly persuasive.
Even if in the end there is nothing to it, it doesn't matter.
It is very persuasive to us.
So Buddha began with suffering.
And little by little over the generations, Buddhism worked its way up to the cosmos.
And our Western traditions begin from the opposite perspective.
We begin with the cosmos and work our way down to poor, pathetic human beings.
So for our traditions, we start with the question of God, the ultimate, the eternal, the cosmic.
It's really important.
It wasn't important to Buddha.
It wasn't that the Buddha denied God, it's just that for him it seemed like a blind alley.
So nothing in Buddhism is called empty, or emptiness, shunyata.

The word shunyata actually means something like swollen, in the sense of a big balloon that's swollen and round and looks substantial, but actually there's nothing inside, and it's the very nothing inside that makes the balloon what it is.
If there weren't that nothing inside, you wouldn't have the balloon, right?
So the balloon looks like something to worry about, but there's nothing to worry about because there's nothing there.
The analogy, of course, is not perfect because inside the balloon, as we know now, there's not nothing.
There's air, and air is already something.
But emptiness means there isn't anything inside the balloon, and that's what makes it a balloon.
You have this formula all the time in the Diamond Sutra, where it says many times, giving, there's no giving, no such thing as giving.
That's why we call it giving.
X is not X.
X is nothing, and that's why we call it X.
It's thanks to nothing that everything is, thanks to nothing that things can grow, can develop, can change.
Change is completely inevitable, of course.
Where there's being, there's change.
That's pretty much the definition of being: change.
And change is wonderful and terrible.
Change is growth and development and exciting new things, and change is loss and abandonment.
These things are exactly the same thing.
Growth, development is loss.
Loss is growth and development.
The only reason we give them different names is because we like one and we don't like the other one, so we have to have different names.
But they're the same.
They're nothing.
They're emptiness.
But, of course, in Buddhism, it's not exactly that emptiness is nothing.
In Buddhism, they call nothing nihilism, and they call something eternalism.
These are considered to be extreme views.
Emptiness is something that's neither nihilism nor eternalism.
It's something in between.
It's neither nothing nor something.
And, of course, there also is no emptiness either.
Emptiness isn't a state or an insight or an ontological reality.
It's just a word used to indicate how the world of our experience, of our living, actually is.
It's not as we see it.
It's not as we grasp it.
It's not as we worry about it.
It's not as we are oppressed by it.
It's not like that.
It's empty, free of any binding, free of any pain.
Emptiness is connection.
That's why things are empty.
Because when you look for something, you don't really find it.
You can sit for the rest of the week and try to find you.
You don't find you.
You find thoughts, feelings, sensations, perceptions.
You find some consciousness, but you don't really find any you.
You only find connection, because everything causes everything else.
There is nothing that could ever arise without everything else.
Of course, this is totally obvious.
If there's no universe, there's no you.
If there's no earth, no sky, there's no you.
And there's no me.
And there's no me without you and all of those who have made me.
There's no you without me.
There's no language in the world that has the word you and not the word me.
And this is exactly emptiness.
If you look for yourself, you won't find yourself.
You'll only find everyone else and everything else that made you.
So emptiness is the opposite of cold and distant and foreboding and philosophical.
Emptiness is the most intimate possible thing.
Emptiness is compassion.
It's ease and kindness and caring and absolute continuous belonging.

I mentioned her.

She was our...

Great.

Very ready.

Good friend.

The last time I saw her she said, oh no, you made me into a saint.
That's terrible.

It's called Seeds for a Boundless Life.
It's a book like Zen Mind Beginner's Mind.

*There is nothing missing.
All the teachers I know have emphasized that we practice for the sake of practice.
Just to express and actualize our intrinsic Buddha nature for the benefit of all beings.
There is nothing we need to get that's not already right here, right now.
In this very body of mind, just as it is.

It's really good for nothing.
And that's right.
Zazen is exactly good for nothing.
It's the best way I know of.
Nothing.
Practice.

*A phrase that Blanche repeated over and over again.
Again, suggesting that everything we need is right here.
To seek for something other than just this.
Implies that something is missing.
That we are not complete, somehow.
The first time I heard Suzuki Roshi speak, he said, You are perfect, just as you are.
And I thought, well, I'm new here, he doesn't know me.
But again and again, he would keep pointing in that direction, saying you have everything you need.
You are already complete.
Just to be alive is enough.
And finally, I had to assume that I was not the sole exception to these assertions.
But I was still dubious.
And as I continued to practice and to talk with other students of the Buddha Dharma, I felt that many people share the conditioning.
That leads us to think that there is something wrong with us.
If only we could get or do or be something more, then we would be alright.
It's so easy for us to get the idea that there is something wrong with us.
And it's so hard to let go of that and just appreciate this one life as it is, as a gift.
In fact, not only is life a gift and practice a gift, everything we have, without exception, has come to us through the kindness of others.*
This one is called, All Beings Have Wisdom and Compassion.
*We have both faith and vow, which together with practice, I have found to be the three main supports of my life.
It is faith that all beings have the wisdom and compassion of the awakened ones, but because of their attachments and delusions, they don't realize it.
So even though we are already complete, because of our attachments and delusions, we need a lot of effort to actualize the wisdom and compassion that is our basic nature.
And that's where devotion comes in.
By entering the Buddha way, we enter a life of vow.
Beings are numberless, I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless, I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to become it.
This is a big vow.
How could we do this?
It must be an endless vow.
When I first came to practice, I thought, I'm a mess now, but I'm going to get straightened out.
And then I'll go on with my life.
After some years, I realized, oh, I'm never going to get done with this.
And I was disappointed for a moment.
But then I thought, Pollyanna, that I am.
Oh, this means you'll never use up this practice.
It'll never wear out.
It'll last my whole life.*
And it did.
It lasted her whole life.
All those years.
*And this is true of our vow.
Our vow will sustain us and inspire us to practice for the rest of our life.
And maybe even for lives to come.
These vows will be our guide and our support and our inspiration for our whole life.*
I'll close with this last short one.
*Being home.
Find your home, wherever you are.
To realize that wherever you are is home.
Not to be seeking for some special place, to be making some cozy nest.
But to find yourself at home, wherever you are and then in whatever circumstances you may be.
To put aside the worldly concerns of looking for material comfort and instead to cultivate mental comfort, comfort of the spirit and the mind and heart.
This being at home, wherever you are, means being comfortable wherever you are.
Not having to have some special place or special things to make you comfortable.
Right here.
In this very body.
In this very place as it is.
Is home.*
So maybe, Blanche breathed in and she breathed out and then she really went home.
Simple.
It's wonderful, Blanche's words.
So simple.
Not fancy.
